extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, theology students, moral theologians, and Catholic clergy
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic theological exposition of the Catholic doctrine concerning the meritoriousness of good works: its biblical and patristic foundations, the requisites (conditions) for true merit, the agent's and God's roles, and the objects (rewards) of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation of the meritoriousness of good works
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church affirms that good works performed in the state of sanctifying grace are meritorious; this teaching is attested by Councils (Second Council of Orange, Fourth Lateran, Tridentine Council) and by Scripture and Tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites conciliar texts (e.g., Tridentine canon: life eternal proposed 'as a grace ... and as a reward ... to be faithfully rendered to their good works and merits'); Scriptural passages (Wisdom V, Beatitudes, Rom II, 2 Tim IV, 1 Cor III, Col III, James, Apocalypse) and Patristic witnesses (Ignatius, Irenaeus, Ambrose, Augustine) are given as foundation; also notes condemnations of contrary positions (e.g., certain Lutheran and quietistic errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 1 — Work must be morally good (opus honestum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work to be meritorious must be morally good; evil deeds are demeritorious and cannot merit reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support cited (Eph VI, 2 Cor V); explanation that there are virtually no morally indifferent works 'in individuo' and that even works of obligation (observance of commandments) are meritorious; notes uncertainty whether mere omission of an evil act is meritorious and that external work adds merit mainly insofar as it sustains the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 2 — Moral liberty (libertas indifferens ad actum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit requires freedom from external and internal compulsion; the act must be an actus humanus freely performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogmatically defined against Jansenius. Scriptural examples (1 Cor IX, Matt XIX). Explains the necessary species of liberty (libertas contradictionis sive exercitii) and distinguishes cases (e.g., hypothetical cases where physical freedom without genuine moral choice may lack merit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 3 — Actual grace (prevenient and cooperating grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be meritorious an act must be supernatural and therefore requires the assistance of actual grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues necessity from the supernatural character of meritorious acts; the act cannot be meritorious without prevenient and cooperating grace. No specific scriptural citations beyond general theological argumentation in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 4 — Supernatural motive (motivo supernatural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit requires a supernatural motive: good works must be supernatural in object, circumstances, and end; theologians debate precisely which supernatural motive is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two major schools described: (α) Rigorous Thomist view demanding the motive of theological charity (caritas) for each meritorious act (some insist on actual act of charity 'toties quoties'); majority Thomists accept influxus virtualis caritatis (virtual influence of charity suffices) and Bellarmine's insistence on referring each act to God. (β) Suarez, Vasquez, De Lugo, Ballerini: if the agent has habitual charity, conformity to divine law suffices and no special motive is required. Scriptural and practical implications discussed (Beatitudes, keeping commandments). Practical recommendation: frequent acts of charity and making a 'good intention' daily to increase meritoriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 5 — Agent must be in the wayfaring state (status viae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only works performed during earthly life (the 'wayfaring' state) can merit; death closes the time of meriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support: sowing in this world to reap in the next; emphasizes that meriting is limited to life on earth and that death is the natural limit of meriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 6 — Agent must be in the state of sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the just (those in sanctifying grace) can merit; sanctifying grace is a necessary condition of meritoriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations (John XV, Rom VIII). Discusses whether degree of sanctifying grace affects quantity of merit: majority (with St. Thomas) holds greater sanctifying grace increases meritoriousness of the same act, though some (Vasquez) deny greater merit for holier agents. Explains why intercession of saints sometimes obtains greater favors for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite 7 — Divine acceptance/promise (in actu secundo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit requires God's acceptance of the good work 'in actu secundo' and (for some schools) God's gratuitous promise to reward; theologians differ on the role of divine acceptance versus intrinsic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three theological positions outlined: Scotists — condignitas rests entirely on God's gratuitous promise/acceptance; Suarez school — merit has equality with reward by strict justice (God obliged ex iustitia); Lessius/Vasquez/De Lugo — condignitas owes both to intrinsic value of work and to God's free acceptance/promise (preferred here). Scriptural and patristic arguments (James, Augustine) invoked; author favors the mixed view that respects intrinsic value yet grounds the divine obligation in God's truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of merit — Increase of sanctifying grace (gratia secunda)
rubrics_metrics.description: One object of merit is the augmentation of sanctifying grace (gratia secunda); the first grace of justification (gratia prima) cannot be strictly merited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes gratia prima (not meritable) from gratia secunda (can be increased by good works). Discusses that actual efficacious graces (and final perseverance) cannot be strictly merited, though merely sufficient graces may be merited de condigno; cites the Tridentine Council's teaching on gratuity of justification and warns against a vicious circle if first graces were merited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of merit — Eternal life / heavenly glory (gloria prima) and its attainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Eternal life (heavenly glory) is an object of merit; the attainment of eternal life is conditioned ('si tamen in gratia decesserit') — i.e., one must die in grace to receive the reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes Tridentine phrasing distinguishing 'eternal life' and 'attainment of eternal life'; explains that loss of sanctifying grace at death forfeits previously acquired merits. Discusses debates whether gloria prima can be merited (distinguishing infants, baptized adults, catechumens, and those justified by perfect contrition) and the relation of sacramental effects to claims to glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of merit — Increase of heavenly glory (gloria secunda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good works can merit an increase of heavenly glory — a differentiated, unequal share of glory among the elect corresponds to differing measures of grace and meritorious works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support (Matt XVI, 1 Cor III); explains causal link: good works augment grace, which grounds inequalities of glory in heaven; thus meritorious works performed on earth are causally linked to differing heavenly rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: meritum de condigno versus meritum de congruo
rubrics_metrics.description: Condign merit (meritum de condigno) gives a strict claim in justice to reward; congruous merit (meritum de congruo) gives only a quasi-claim based on equity or decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the two are not species of one genus but analogous; some scholastics (Dominicus Soto, Becanus) rejected 'meritum de congruo' due to ambiguity of 'equity' but the text defends the term. Discusses historical Semipelagian debate and Augustine's nuanced recognition that justifying faith of the sinner is not entirely without merit (contextualizing congruous merit).
